findings.actualVisibleFacts: Two horizontal levels, left upward arrow from lower to upper level, right downward arrow from upper to lower level. The downward arrow is the one explicitly labelled e−. Both sit above the sole caption Elektronenanregung.
findings.scientificAssessment: An upward transition is compatible with absorption/excitation. A downward transition represents relaxation/de-excitation, not excitation. Both arrows can form a valid excitation/relaxation pair if separately identified; the common excitation caption and e− on the downward branch do not communicate that distinction. Therefore this is a concrete instructional ambiguity, not proof that the image contains only a wrong downward arrow.
findings.minimumCorrection: Either retain only an unmistakably upward labelled absorption/excitation transition, or label upward Absorption/Anregung and downward Relaxation/Abregung separately. Do not label the downward process excitation. No need to add an unrequested detailed emission model.

findings.actualVisibleFacts: The fill runs from violet/blue at short wavelengths to yellow/orange/red at the600-nm apex, then returns through orange to yellow near700nm.
findings.scientificAssessment: On an increasing wavelength axis the visible spectral order proceeds toward red at the long-wave end. A red-to-yellow return toward700nm is not a physical wavelength-colour map. The fill has no legend marking it decorative, and the adjoining colour interpretation encourages treating the colours as wavelengths. This creates a misleading visual encoding even though the peak position itself is correct.
findings.minimumCorrection: Use a neutral single fill for the illustrative absorbance band, or a monotonic physically ordered wavelength colour strip/fill with appropriate approximate ranges. Keep the600-nm apex and axes if retained.

findings.actualVisibleFacts: The plot labels lambda_max approximately600nm; the card says absorption of red light and complementary colour blue, alongside a blue sample.
findings.scientificAssessment: Around600nm is conventionally orange; a broad band centred there can also absorb some red light and a blue-looking solution is qualitatively plausible. It would be wrong to claim red absorption is absent or that the blue sample alone is disproved. However the explicit red/blue pair as the explanation of the600-nm example is imprecise and suppresses the dependence on the whole absorption band and illumination.
findings.minimumCorrection: Align the illustrative caption with the actual band, for example predominantly orange light near600nm and approximately blue appearance under white illumination. State the schematic/approximate nature instead of implying exact colour from lambda_max alone.
